idea: A giant semicolon in an old Venetian roman, with tiny type beneath: 'Not finished; just pausing. First printed in Venice, 1496.' The semicolon first appeared in print in Aldus Manutius's edition of Bembo's De Aetna, so it's a punctuation-nerd shirt that also says you're not done yet.

The word 'italic' set in a slanting Aldine italic, captioned 'Leaning in since 1501.' Aldus Manutius and his punchcutter Francesco Griffo brought italic type into print with their 1501 Virgil. It's a nice dry joke for people who know where the slant came from.

A large ampersand built so you can see the 'e' and 't' of Latin 'et' inside it, captioned 'and per se and'. Schoolchildren once recited '& per se and' at the end of the alphabet, and that phrase slurred into the word 'ampersand'. It's a pretty glyph with a hidden etymology.

One unbroken block of Roman capitals: 'INANTIQUITYMOSTTEXTSHADNOSPACESBETWEENWORDSANDREADERSCOPED'. Scriptio continua, writing without word spaces, was normal in classical Latin and Greek manuscripts. It reads like a puzzle and quietly reminds you that word spaces were invented.

The test word 'Hamburgefonstiv' set huge in a clean grotesque, with a small line: 'The first word a typeface learns.' Type designers use it because its letters cover most of the basic shapes in a lowercase alphabet. It's an insider word that also looks good as pure letterforms.

Samuel Johnson's own dictionary entry, set as in 1755: 'LEXICO'GRAPHER. n.s. A writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.' It's a famous self-deprecating line from the man who wrote the dictionary, for editors, writers and anyone who loves careful work nobody notices.

A dictionary-style entry: 'nice (adj.) 1. foolish, ignorant [from Latin nescius, 'not knowing']. 2. pleasant. — Words change their minds too.' 'Nice' really did mean silly or foolish in Middle English. It's a polite-looking shirt that's secretly a small insult.

A big interrobang ‽ with the caption 'Invented 1962. Still waiting for its moment‽' The advertising man Martin K. Speckter proposed the combined ?! mark in 1962, and it never quite caught on. It's an elegant glyph with a deadpan joke about its own obscurity.

A row of four glyphs: a Proto-Sinaitic ox head, Phoenician aleph, Greek alpha, and a Roman A, captioned 'Every A is an ox, upside down.' The letter A comes from the Semitic 'aleph', 'ox', and it rotated as it passed between scripts. It's a 3,500-year history in one line of letters.

A large pilcrow ¶ with the caption 'Before line breaks, there was this.' Medieval scribes marked new thoughts inside running text with the pilcrow, before it became normal to start paragraphs on a new line. It's a shapely mark with a story only text people know.

A single ivy-leaf hedera ❦, captioned 'Hedera. Dividing thoughts since antiquity.' The ivy-leaf mark shows up as a word and section divider in ancient Greek and Latin inscriptions, long before printers used it as a fleuron. It's minimal and botanical, and it fits right next to the Haeckel plates.

Three marks lined up with their names: '-  hyphen   –  en dash   —  em dash', and below: 'Know the difference.' The em dash is traditionally as wide as the type's point size and the en dash half that. It's a clean specimen that doubles as a stance for editors and fussy writers.

Lines of text with the gaps between them labelled 'leading (rhymes with sledding): the strips of lead printers put between lines.' The word comes straight from hand-set metal type. It's a small, beautifully spaced shirt that's quietly about breathing room.

Two drawn printer's type cases, the top one full of CAPITALS and the bottom one of lowercase, captioned 'Capitals lived upstairs.' Compositors kept majuscules in the upper case and minuscules in the lower, which is where the terms come from. It's architecture and etymology in one diagram.

A giant manicule ☞ pointing at the word 'this.' in small type, captioned 'Manicule: the reader's finger in the margin, 12th–18th c.' Readers really did draw little pointing hands next to passages that mattered to them. It's charming, a little bossy, and about paying attention.

The scribe's colophon in a manuscript book hand: 'Explicit hoc totum; pro Christo da mihi potum.', translated below as 'That's the whole thing. For Christ's sake, give me a drink.' Medieval copyists really did end manuscripts with rhymes like this one. It shows the tired human behind every old book.

An asterism ⁂ set large and centred, captioned 'Asterism. For when one asterisk isn't enough.' It's a real, nearly forgotten typographic mark once used to set off sections or point to a note. It reads as a small constellation, and it's a deep cut for book people.

The word 'CLUE' with a thread-like line running out of the 'C', and the etymology: 'from clew: a ball of thread (see Theseus, labyrinth).' The modern word comes from 'clew', the ball of yarn that led Theseus out of the Minotaur's maze. It's a mystery-lover's shirt with a myth inside.

'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet' set like a grand classical inscription, with the footnote 'Cicero, mangled. De finibus bonorum et malorum, 45 BC.' The world's favourite placeholder text is a garbled passage of Cicero, about the pursuit of pain and pleasure. It's for designers who like knowing what their filler actually says.

A column of 42 lines of blackletter text, with only '42 lines. Mainz, c. 1455.' under it. Gutenberg's Bible is called the 42-line Bible after the number of lines in most of its columns, and it was the first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type. It's a dense, beautiful texture marking where printing began.
